audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is EIP-7702 authorization nonce properly validated to prevent same-chain replay attacks?

observations: Nonce validation at line 594-596 compares authorization nonce against account's current nonce
Nonce overflow check at line 578-579 prevents uint64 overflow
Validation occurs BEFORE signature verification in the code flow

phase2_findings.property_analysis: The nonce validation correctly enforces that authorization.nonce must equal the authorizer's current account nonce. This prevents same-chain replay because after successful application, the nonce is incremented (line 616 in applyAuthorization).
edge_cases_analyzed: nonce rollover: Not possible due to overflow check

phase3_classification.rationale: The implementation correctly validates that the authorization nonce matches the account's current nonce before processing. The nonce increment after successful authorization ensures each authorization can only be used once. Overflow protection is in place.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-020: Does encode_account receive a correct 32-byte storage_root Merkle root from all callers?
audit_items.rationale: This check references a Python specification function (encode_account) from the Ethereum execution-specs. The geth codebase uses a different architecture for account encoding via the trie package.

audit_items.title: Can type alias constructors (Address, Root, VersionedHash, Bloom) be bypassed to create instances with incorrect byte lengths?

observations: Go's fixed-size arrays enforce length at compile time
Type safety is enforced by Go's type system

phase3_classification.rationale: Go's type system with fixed-size arrays provides compile-time enforcement of byte lengths. These types cannot be instantiated with incorrect lengths.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-018: Does parse_deposit_requests enforce deterministic receipt key ordering across all execution clients?

phase3_classification.rationale: Deposit log ordering is deterministic because it follows block transaction order and within-transaction log emission order. All compliant EL clients must execute transactions in block order.

audit_items.title: Verify execution client consensus: Do all compliant execution clients produce identical requests_hash for the same block?
audit_items.rationale: This check requires cross-client testing (Geth, Nethermind, Besu, Erigon). This is an integration/conformance test, not a code audit item.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does trie_get properly validate and handle missing receipt keys from untrusted P2P blocks?
audit_items.rationale: The trie_get function referenced is from the Python execution-specs. In geth, receipt validation happens during block import via receipts root hash comparison.

audit_items.title: Is the receipts trie integrity validated before parse_deposit_requests processes receipt keys?

phase3_classification.rationale: The receipts trie integrity is validated via receipts root comparison during block validation, which occurs before ParseDepositLogs is called.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-022: Can an attacker forge a transaction signature that recovers to a different sender address?

phase3_classification.rationale: The signature validation enforces proper bounds on r, s values and the s-value lower half requirement (EIP-2). The libsecp256k1 library provides robust ECDSA recovery.

audit_items.title: Verify Execution Client Transaction Authentication: Does the execution client properly validate recovered sender addresses?

phase3_classification.rationale: The client performs independent sender recovery using the signature and never trusts externally-provided sender addresses.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-006/tb-001: Is ECDSA signature verification correctly enforced for all EIP-7702 Authorization tuples?

phase3_classification.rationale: EIP-7702 authorization signature verification correctly uses ecrecover with the proper message hash. Signature malleability is prevented by enforcing s <= secp256k1n/2.

audit_items.title: Verify EIP-7702 Authorizer Authentication: Can an attacker forge authorization to impersonate the actor-eip7702-authorizer?

phase3_classification.rationale: The authorizer address is cryptographically derived from the signature via ecrecover. Without the private key, an attacker cannot produce a signature that recovers to the victim's address.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-006: Is the ECDSA signature s-value validated to be in the lower half of secp256k1 curve order?

phase3_classification.rationale: The ValidateSignatureValues function with homestead=true explicitly checks s <= secp256k1n/2. This is the correct implementation of EIP-2 signature malleability protection.

audit_items.title: Does signature malleability in EIP-7702 Authorization allow recovery to an unintended address?

phase3_classification.rationale: Signature malleability cannot cause recovery to an unintended address because the s-value check ensures only one signature form is valid.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does the EIP-7702 authorization validation correctly reject ecrecover results returning address(0)?

phase3_classification.rationale: Unlike Solidity's ecrecover which returns zero address on failure, Go's crypto.Ecrecover returns errors. Additional validation checks for empty/malformed public keys provide defense in depth.

audit_items.title: Is the transaction sender validation robust against address(0) authorization attacks at the P2P boundary?

phase3_classification.rationale: Invalid authorizations are skipped per EIP-7702 specification. The zero-address attack vector doesn't exist because Go's Ecrecover returns errors rather than zero addresses.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is the EIP-7702 Authorization chain_id field validated against the current chain ID?

phase3_classification.rationale: Chain ID validation correctly implements EIP-7702 specification. The wildcard (chain_id=0) is intentional and documented.

audit_items.title: Does the EIP-7702 Authorizer actor enforce chain_id binding before signing delegation authorizations?

phase3_classification.rationale: The chain_id is included in the signed message hash, providing cryptographic binding.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-006: Is EIP-7702 Authorization nonce validation correctly enforced?

phase3_classification.rationale: Nonce validation is correctly enforced: exact match required, overflow protected, checked before state changes.

audit_items.title: Can an attacker replay an EIP-7702 Authorization after the authorizer's nonce has incremented?

phase3_classification.rationale: Replay protection is correctly implemented via nonce increment. After successful authorization, the nonce advances, making the original authorization invalid for replay.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-006: Is the authorizer's nonce incremented after successful EIP-7702 authorization processing?

phase3_classification.rationale: Nonce is correctly incremented after successful authorization processing at line 616.

audit_items.title: Verify EIP-7702 Authorization Replay Protection: Can the same authorization be accepted twice?

phase3_classification.rationale: The nonce mechanism prevents double-acceptance. The exact-match requirement ensures each authorization is single-use.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-001: Is the resolution of multiple EIP-7702 Authorizations targeting the same authorizer deterministic?

phase3_classification.rationale: The processing is deterministic: authorizations are applied in array order, and the nonce mechanism ensures only the first valid authorization for an account succeeds.

audit_items.title: Does the transaction sender have the ability to craft authorization sequences that produce implementation-specific behavior?

phase3_classification.rationale: EIP-7702 fully specifies the authorization processing order and error handling. The implementation follows this specification.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does parse_deposit_requests validate BOTH log.address AND log.topics[0]?

phase3_classification.rationale: Both address and topic validation are correctly implemented with logical AND. This prevents deposit spoofing from contracts at different addresses.

audit_items.title: Verify Deposit Contract Address Integrity: Is DEPOSIT_CONTRACT_ADDRESS correctly defined and immutable?

phase3_classification.rationale: The deposit contract address is immutably defined in chain configuration. Runtime modification is not possible.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does parse_deposit_requests correctly filter logs by topic before processing?

phase3_classification.rationale: Topic filtering is correctly implemented with proper bounds checking (len > 0 before access) and exact topic matching.

audit_items.title: Verify Deposit Contract Log Integrity: Can a malicious transaction cause the deposit contract to emit logs that bypass topic filtering?

phase3_classification.rationale: The deposit contract can only emit its defined events. Attackers cannot cause the deposit contract to emit logs with different topics.

audit_items.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does extract_deposit_data correctly reject deposit event data where length != 576 bytes?

phase3_classification.rationale: The length validation is correctly implemented with an exact-match check (len != 576).

audit_items.title: Verify Deposit Contract Event Handling: Are malformed deposit events from the EL node properly validated at the trust boundary?

phase3_classification.rationale: Length validation is enforced before any parsing. Invalid deposit data causes block rejection.
